quote: Wenn man eine Gleichung mit ganzzahligen Coefficienten [-A-] hat und man transformirt rational [-xx-], ist dann auch der wesentliche Theiler der Diskriminante die hinreichende Invariante?
english: If one has an equation with integer coefficients and one transforms it rationally, is the essential divisor of the discriminant then also the sufficient invariant?
topic: Notes on asking for necessary and sufficient criteria for equations to have equal roots using only equations rather than inequalities, a plan to prove that the functions of a finite integrality domain divisible by given forms again form a finite integrality domain, and a question on whether the essential part of the discriminant is the sufficient invariant under rational transformation of equations with integer coefficients.

triage.modern_statement: Take an irreducible polynomial f with integer coefficients and its number field K = Q(θ). Apply rational (Tschirnhaus) transformations θ ↦ g(θ), with g having rational coefficients. The polynomial discriminant then changes by square factors (the 'inessential' part, which comes from the index). The 'essential divisor' (Kronecker's wesentlicher Teiler) stays the same: it is the field discriminant d_K. The question is whether d_K is a complete invariant. In other words, if two such equations have the same essential discriminant divisor, must they be rationally transformable into each other, i.e. define isomorphic (conjugate) number fields?
triage.answered_by: No single person resolved it; the answer 'no' became standard knowledge in algebraic number theory. Different number fields can share a discriminant. A simple case: for squarefree D, a cubic field of discriminant D and its 3-isomorphic companion fields (counted by the 3-rank of the class group of Q(√D)) all have discriminant D. Hermite's finiteness theorem says only finitely many fields share a given discriminant, but that number can exceed one. A strong form is Perlis (1977): arithmetically equivalent fields have the same Dedekind zeta function, so the same degree and discriminant, without being isomorphic.

evidence.claim: Many non-isomorphic number fields can have the same discriminant D. For example, if D is squarefree and K is a cubic field of discriminant D, other cubic fields can share it.
By a well-known result of Perlis, arithmetically equivalent number fields have the same degree and discriminant. The paper studies non-conjugate number fields that share a discriminant.
Arithmetically equivalent number fields are not necessarily isomorphic, but they always have the same degree, discriminant, signature and Galois closure.

Kronecker's split of the discriminant into essential and inessential (ausserwesentlich) divisors, and the problem of common inessential discriminant divisors, are documented in histories of algebraic number theory (Dedekind, Hensel, Kronecker).
The field discriminant is a basic invariant of a number field, and only finitely many fields have a given discriminant (Hermite).

triage.why: I am reading 'wesentlicher Theiler der Diskriminante' as Kronecker's essential discriminant divisor, i.e. the field discriminant. It is the part that survives rational transformation, while index factors are inessential. Under that reading, the question asks whether the field discriminant alone classifies the equations up to rational transformation. Standard results give a negative answer: there are counterexamples among cubic fields, and Perlis's arithmetically equivalent fields are a further case. This is not one of Hilbert's 23 problems or the 24th problem. Some uncertainty remains: '[-A-]' and '[-xx-]' are illegible gaps in the source, and Hilbert could have meant a narrower sense of 'sufficient invariant' that I cannot recover. Related questions (when discriminant, trace form or zeta function determine the field) are still studied, but that work does not address this note directly.
